topics.title: Basics of Physics — Mechanics, Heat, Waves & Optics
topics.theory:
- **Units & measurements**: SI base units are metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela; **dimensional analysis** checks formula consistency (work = ML²T⁻²).
- **Newton's laws**: F = ma (**second law**); every action has an equal and opposite reaction (**third law**, e.g. rocket propulsion); **inertia** is resistance to change of motion.
- **Equations of motion** (constant acceleration): v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as.
- **Work** W = Fd cosθ, **kinetic energy** = ½mv², **power** = work/time (SI unit **watt**); energy is conserved, and momentum is conserved in an isolated system.
- **Gravitation**: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth; **escape velocity** of Earth ≈ 11.2 km/s; **Archimedes' principle** gives buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced.
- **Heat & temperature**: Q = mcΔT; specific heat of water ≈ 4200 J/kg·K; K = °C + 273; heat flows by **conduction, convection, radiation** (radiation needs no medium).
- **Latent heat**: temperature stays constant during a phase change; water has maximum density at **4 °C**.
- **Waves & sound**: v = fλ; sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave needing a medium; audible range 20 Hz–20 kHz; speed in air ≈ 340 m/s; **Doppler effect** changes apparent frequency.
- **Light**: speed in vacuum 3 × 10⁸ m/s; **refractive index** n = c/v; **total internal reflection** (denser to rarer, angle above critical) drives optical fibres.
- **Mirrors & lenses**: f = R/2 for spherical mirrors; lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f; power P = 1/f (metres) in **dioptre**; myopia is corrected by a concave lens, hypermetropia by a convex lens.

qs.stem: The SI unit of force is
qs.sol: Force = mass × acceleration, so its unit is kg·m/s², named the newton. Joule is energy, pascal is pressure and watt is power; an examiner may next ask for their dimensional formulas.

qs.stem: The dimensional formula of work is
qs.sol: Work = force × distance = (MLT⁻²)(L) = ML²T⁻². MLT⁻² is force, ML²T⁻³ is power and ML⁻¹T⁻² is pressure.

qs.stem: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 5 s. The distance covered is
qs.sol: s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 2 × 25 = 25 m. The final speed is v = at = 10 m/s; 10 m would be the speed and 50 m is the wrong v × t.

qs.stem: A net force of 10 N acts on a body of mass 2 kg. Its acceleration is
qs.sol: By Newton's second law a = F/m = 10/2 = 5 m/s². Expect a follow-up on how acceleration changes if mass is doubled.

qs.stem: Which phenomenon is a direct illustration of Newton's third law of motion?

opts.A: A passenger jerked forward when a bus brakes suddenly
opts.B: Rocket moving forward by expelling hot gases backward
opts.C: A ball rolling and gradually stopping on rough ground
opts.D: A heavier cart needing more force for the same acceleration

qs.sol: The rocket pushes gas backward and the gas pushes the rocket forward with an equal and opposite force. The bus jerk shows inertia (first law) and the cart example shows F = ma (second law).

qs.stem: The kinetic energy of a 2 kg body moving at 3 m/s is
qs.sol: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J. Doubling the speed would quadruple KE, a common follow-up.

qs.stem: The approximate escape velocity from the surface of the Earth is
qs.sol: Escape velocity ve = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s. 7.9 km/s is the orbital velocity near the surface, 9.8 is g in m/s² and 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light.

qs.stem: Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force on a body immersed in a fluid equals

opts.A: the volume of the body multiplied by its mass
opts.B: the pressure of the fluid at the surface
opts.D: the weight of the fluid displaced by the body

qs.sol: Upthrust equals the weight of the displaced fluid; a body floats when this equals its own weight. The next question could be about the density condition for floating.

qs.stem: A force of 20 N moves a body 5 m in a direction making 60° with the force. The work done is (cos 60° = 0.5)
qs.sol: W = Fd cosθ = 20 × 5 × 0.5 = 50 J. 100 J ignores the angle, which applies when the force is along the displacement.

qs.stem: A machine does 600 J of work in 20 s. Its power is
qs.sol: Power = work/time = 600/20 = 30 W. Remember that 1 horsepower is about 746 W.

qs.stem: The heat needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 °C (specific heat 4200 J/kg·K) is
qs.sol: Q = mcΔT = 2 × 4200 × 10 = 84000 J. Examiners may reverse the problem and ask for the final temperature or mass.

qs.stem: A temperature of 27 °C on the Kelvin scale is
qs.sol: K = °C + 273 = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Absolute zero is 0 K, i.e. about −273 °C.

qs.stem: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth mainly by
qs.sol: Radiation transfers energy by electromagnetic waves and needs no material medium, unlike conduction and convection. Space between Sun and Earth is nearly vacuum.

qs.stem: While ice melts at its melting point, the supplied heat

opts.A: is absorbed as latent heat and the temperature remains constant
opts.B: raises the temperature of the ice-water mixture steadily
opts.C: is lost to the surroundings entirely
opts.D: is converted into kinetic energy of the container

qs.sol: During a phase change the heat goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into raising temperature. Latent heat of fusion of ice is about 336 kJ/kg.

qs.stem: Water has its maximum density at
qs.sol: Water anomalously contracts from 0 to 4 °C and expands above 4 °C, so it is densest at 4 °C; this lets aquatic life survive under frozen lakes.

qs.stem: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz has a wavelength of 0.68 m. The speed of the wave is
qs.sol: v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m/s, the typical speed of sound in air. Remember that sound is faster in solids than in gases.

qs.stem: Sound cannot travel through
qs.sol: Sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave and needs a material medium. It travels fastest in solids such as steel, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.

qs.stem: The audible range of frequencies for a normal human ear is
qs.sol: Below 20 Hz is infrasound and above 20 kHz is ultrasound. Dogs and bats can hear ultrasonic frequencies.

qs.stem: A person hears an echo 2 s after shouting at a cliff. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, the cliff is at a distance of
qs.sol: Sound travels to the cliff and back, so the distance is (340 × 2)/2 = 340 m. 680 m wrongly uses the total path.

qs.stem: When a source of sound moves towards a stationary observer, the observer hears

opts.C: the same frequency but louder amplitude

qs.sol: Waves are compressed in front of an approaching source, increasing apparent frequency (Doppler effect). A receding source gives lower pitch; the speed of sound in the medium does not change.

qs.stem: The speed of light in vacuum is approximately
qs.sol: c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s (299,792,458 m/s exactly). Light takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth from the Sun.

qs.stem: Light travels at 2 × 10⁸ m/s in a transparent medium. Its refractive index (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s) is
qs.sol: n = c/v = 3 × 10⁸ / 2 × 10⁸ = 1.5, typical of glass. Refractive index is never less than 1 for ordinary media, so 0.67 is impossible.

qs.stem: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels

opts.A: from a rarer to a denser medium at any angle
opts.B: from a denser to a rarer medium at normal incidence
opts.C: between two media of equal refractive index
opts.D: from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle

qs.sol: Both conditions are required: denser-to-rarer travel and incidence beyond the critical angle. Optical fibres and mirages rely on it.

qs.stem: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. Its focal length is
qs.sol: For spherical mirrors f = R/2 = 20 cm. Related: a plane mirror has infinite focal length.

qs.stem: A convex lens has a focal length of 50 cm. Its power is
qs.sol: P = 1/f with f in metres = 1/0.5 = +2 D. A concave lens would have negative power.

qs.stem: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
qs.sol: A convex mirror always forms an erect, virtual, diminished image and gives a wide field of view. Concave mirrors are used in shaving mirrors and headlights.

qs.stem: Myopia (short-sightedness) is corrected by using a
qs.sol: In myopia the image forms in front of the retina, so a diverging (concave) lens is used. Hypermetropia needs a convex lens.

qs.stem: A rainbow is formed in the sky mainly due to

opts.A: dispersion and internal reflection of sunlight in water droplets
opts.B: scattering of light by dust particles only
opts.D: polarisation of light by the atmosphere

qs.sol: Refraction, dispersion and internal reflection inside raindrops separate white light into seven colours. The blue colour of the sky, in contrast, is due to Rayleigh scattering.

qs.stem: An object is placed at 2f from a convex lens. The image formed is

opts.C: real, inverted and of the same size, at 2f on the other side

qs.sol: At u = 2f the lens formula gives v = 2f with magnification −1. This property is used to measure focal length experimentally.

qs.stem: The length of a simple pendulum is increased to four times. Its time period becomes
qs.sol: T = 2π√(L/g), so T ∝ √L; √4 = 2, so the period doubles. The period is independent of the bob's mass.

topics.deep:
- **Units and dimensions**
  - SI has 7 base quantities: length (m), mass (kg), time (s), current (A), temperature (K), amount of substance (mol), luminous intensity (cd).
  - Derived units: force N = kg·m/s², pressure Pa = N/m², energy J = N·m, power W = J/s, frequency Hz = s⁻¹.
  - Dimensional analysis can verify a formula but cannot fix dimensionless constants.
- **Mechanics key formulas**

| Quantity | Formula | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Force | F = ma | newton |
| Momentum | p = mv | kg·m/s |
| Work | W = Fd cosθ | joule |
| Kinetic energy | ½mv² | joule |
| Potential energy | mgh | joule |
| Power | W/t = Fv | watt |
| Pendulum period | T = 2π√(L/g) | second |

  - Uniform acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as. Starting from rest at 2 m/s² for 5 s gives v = 10 m/s and s = 25 m.
  - Conservation: momentum is conserved in all collisions of an isolated system; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions.
  - Escape velocity of Earth is about 11.2 km/s; orbital velocity near surface about 7.9 km/s; it does not depend on the mass of the escaping body.
  - Pendulum period depends on length and g, not on mass; quadrupling the length doubles the period.
- **Fluids**
  - Pressure = force/area; Pascal's law underlies hydraulic lifts; Archimedes' principle explains floating and sinking.
- **Heat**
  - Q = mcΔT; specific heat of water about 4200 J/kg·K (high, so water is a good coolant).
  - Kelvin = Celsius + 273, so 27 °C = 300 K.
  - Conduction (solids, needs contact), convection (fluids, bulk motion), radiation (electromagnetic waves, works in vacuum).
  - During melting or boiling, supplied heat is **latent heat** and temperature stays constant.
  - Water is densest at 4 °C, which is why lakes freeze from the top.
- **Waves and sound**
  - v = fλ for every wave; sound is longitudinal (compressions and rarefactions) and cannot travel in vacuum.
  - Audible 20 Hz–20 kHz; infrasound below 20 Hz; ultrasound above 20 kHz (used in sonography and SONAR).
  - Echo: distance = (speed × time)/2. An echo heard after 2 s at 340 m/s means a reflector 340 m away. Minimum distance for a distinct echo is about 17 m.
  - Doppler effect: source approaching gives higher apparent frequency, receding gives lower.
  - Pitch depends on frequency, loudness on amplitude, quality (timbre) on waveform.
- **Light and optics**
  - Reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. Refraction: Snell's law n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂.
  - n = c/v; light of speed 2 × 10⁸ m/s in a medium gives n = 1.5 (glass).
  - Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle above the critical angle; used in optical fibres, prisms, diamonds' sparkle.
  - Mirrors: f = R/2. Concave mirror: shaving, headlights, telescopes. Convex mirror: rear-view, wide field of view, always virtual and diminished image.
  - Lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f (Cartesian sign). Object at 2f of a convex lens gives a real, inverted image of the same size at 2f.
  - Power P = 1/f in metres; f = 50 cm gives +2 D. Concave lenses have negative power.
  - Eye defects: myopia (concave lens), hypermetropia (convex lens), presbyopia (bifocal).
  - Dispersion by a prism splits white light into VIBGYOR; rainbow = dispersion plus internal reflection in raindrops.
- **Likely question angles:** unit conversions and SI units; quick numeric use of v = u + at, F = ma, Q = mcΔT, v = fλ, f = R/2, P = 1/f; difference between conduction, convection and radiation; echo and Doppler; total internal reflection applications; eye defects and corrective lenses.

topics.title: Basics of Physics — Electricity, Magnetism & Semiconductors
topics.theory:
- **Ohm's law**: V = IR at constant temperature; resistance R = ρL/A, so it grows with length and falls with cross-section; SI unit of resistance is the **ohm**.
- **Series** circuit: R = R₁ + R₂ + ..., same current; **parallel** circuit: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ..., same voltage, total less than the smallest resistor.
- **Electric power** P = VI = I²R = V²/R; energy in **kWh (unit)**, with 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; a **fuse** is placed in series on the live wire.
- **Capacitor**: C = Q/V (farad); parallel capacitors add, series capacitors combine like parallel resistors; stored energy = ½CV².
- **Household supply** in India is 230 V AC at 50 Hz; domestic wiring uses parallel connections with **earthing** for safety.
- **Magnetism**: Oersted showed current produces a magnetic field; **Fleming's left-hand rule** gives force on a conductor (motor effect); field unit is **tesla**, flux unit is **weber**.
- **Electromagnetic induction**: Faraday's law (emf = rate of change of flux) and **Lenz's law** (induced current opposes the change); basis of generators and transformers.
- **Transformer**: works only on AC by mutual induction; Vs/Vp = Ns/Np; step-up has more secondary turns.
- **Semiconductors**: Si and Ge; resistance falls with temperature; **n-type** doping uses pentavalent atoms, **p-type** uses trivalent atoms; PN junction forms a depletion region.
- **Diode** conducts in forward bias (rectifier, silicon drop ≈ 0.7 V); **Zener** regulates voltage; **LED** emits light; **transistor** (emitter, base, collector) amplifies or switches.
- **Modern physics basics**: photon energy E = hν, photoelectric effect (Einstein), radioactive decay with half-life, nuclear fission and fusion.

qs.stem: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 ohm resistor. The current through the resistor is
qs.sol: By Ohm's law I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A. 48 A would come from wrongly multiplying V and R.

qs.stem: Three resistors of 2 ohm, 3 ohm and 5 ohm are connected in series. The equivalent resistance is
qs.sol: Series resistances add: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 ohm. In a series circuit the same current flows through each resistor.

qs.stem: Two resistors of 6 ohm each are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is
qs.sol: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3, so R = 3 ohm. Parallel combination is always less than the smallest individual resistor.

qs.stem: An electric heater is rated 220 V, 5 A. Its power is
qs.sol: P = VI = 220 × 5 = 1100 W. A follow-up could ask the resistance, R = V/I = 44 ohm.

qs.stem: A 2 kW heater is used for 3 hours. The electrical energy consumed is
qs.sol: Energy = power × time = 2 kW × 3 h = 6 kWh, i.e. 6 units. The domestic bill is based on this unit.

qs.stem: Five bulbs of 40 W each are used for 5 hours daily. If one unit costs Rs 7, the daily cost is
qs.sol: Total power = 200 W = 0.2 kW; energy = 0.2 × 5 = 1 kWh = 1 unit, costing Rs 7. Always convert watts to kilowatts before multiplying.

qs.stem: One kilowatt-hour is equal to
qs.sol: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. The kWh is a unit of energy, not of power.

qs.stem: A wire of resistance 10 ohm is replaced by a wire of the same material and cross-section but twice the length. Its resistance becomes
qs.sol: R = ρL/A, so R is proportional to L at constant A; doubling L doubles R to 20 ohm. Doubling the area instead would halve it.

qs.stem: A 10 µF capacitor is charged to 100 V. The charge stored is
qs.sol: Q = CV = 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 = 10⁻³ C = 1 mC. The energy stored is ½CV² = 50 mJ.

qs.stem: Capacitors of 2 µF and 3 µF are connected in parallel. The equivalent capacitance is
qs.sol: Parallel capacitances add: 2 + 3 = 5 µF. In series the result would be 6/5 = 1.2 µF.

qs.stem: Capacitors of 6 µF and 3 µF are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is
qs.sol: 1/C = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so C = 2 µF. Series combination gives less than the smallest capacitor.

qs.stem: The energy stored in a 2 µF capacitor charged to 10 V is
qs.sol: U = ½CV² = ½ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 = 10⁻⁴ J = 100 µJ. A frequent error is forgetting the factor ½ and getting 200 µJ.

qs.stem: In a domestic circuit, a fuse is connected

opts.B: between the live and neutral wires
opts.D: in series with the live wire

qs.sol: A fuse must carry the full circuit current so that it melts on overload and breaks the circuit. It is made of a low-melting-point alloy.

qs.stem: The standard domestic AC supply in India is
qs.sol: India uses 230 V at 50 Hz, while the USA uses about 120 V at 60 Hz. Appliances are connected in parallel.

qs.stem: The magnetic effect of electric current was discovered by
qs.sol: Hans Christian Oersted noticed in 1820 that a current deflects a compass needle. Faraday later discovered electromagnetic induction.

qs.stem: The direction of force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field is given by
qs.sol: The left-hand rule (motor rule) gives the force direction; the right-hand rule gives the direction of induced current in a generator. Mnemonic: left is for motors.

qs.stem: Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of
qs.sol: The induced current opposes the change in flux that produces it; otherwise energy would be created from nothing. It explains the negative sign in Faraday's law.

qs.stem: A transformer has 100 turns in the primary and 500 turns in the secondary. If 20 V AC is applied to the primary, the secondary voltage is
qs.sol: Vs = Vp × Ns/Np = 20 × 500/100 = 100 V, so it is a step-up transformer. Current is correspondingly reduced since power is nearly conserved.

qs.stem: A transformer does not work with a direct current source because

opts.C: DC has a very high frequency
opts.D: a steady current produces no change in magnetic flux

qs.sol: Mutual induction requires a changing flux; a constant DC gives a constant flux and hence no induced emf in the secondary.

qs.stem: The SI unit of magnetic flux is
qs.sol: Flux in weber (Wb); magnetic field (flux density) in tesla = Wb/m². Henry is the unit of inductance.

qs.stem: When the temperature of a semiconductor is increased, its resistance generally
qs.sol: More electron-hole pairs are generated at higher temperatures, increasing conductivity. Metals behave oppositely, with resistance rising with temperature.

qs.stem: A p-type semiconductor is obtained by doping pure silicon with
qs.sol: A trivalent atom leaves a hole, so holes are the majority carriers. Pentavalent atoms such as phosphorus and arsenic give n-type material.

qs.stem: A PN junction diode conducts easily when it is
qs.sol: Forward bias reduces the barrier so majority carriers cross the junction; reverse bias widens the depletion region. This one-way property allows rectification of AC.

qs.stem: The region around a PN junction that is depleted of free charge carriers is called the
qs.sol: Diffusion of electrons and holes leaves immobile ions that form a barrier potential. The width of this layer shrinks in forward bias.

qs.stem: The three terminals of a bipolar junction transistor are
qs.sol: BJT terminals are emitter, base, collector; source, gate and drain belong to a FET. Anode and cathode are the diode terminals.

qs.stem: The approximate forward voltage drop across a conducting silicon diode is
qs.sol: Silicon needs about 0.7 V to begin conducting, germanium about 0.3 V. A follow-up could ask which one is used in a given circuit.

qs.stem: Which device is mainly used as a voltage regulator, operating in reverse breakdown?
qs.sol: A Zener diode maintains a nearly constant voltage across it in reverse breakdown. An LED emits light when forward biased, and a photodiode detects light.

qs.stem: The photoelectric effect was explained by Einstein on the basis of

opts.C: light consisting of quanta (photons) of energy hν

qs.sol: Each photon of energy E = hν can eject one electron if hν exceeds the work function. This supports the particle nature of light.

qs.stem: A radioactive sample of 80 g has a half-life of 10 days. The mass left after 30 days is
qs.sol: 30 days is 3 half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g, i.e. 80/2³. Related: mean life is 1.44 times the half-life.

qs.stem: An electric generator works on the principle of
qs.sol: Rotating a coil in a magnetic field changes flux and induces an emf (Faraday's law). A motor, by contrast, uses the force on a current-carrying conductor.

topics.deep:
- **Current electricity**
  - Current I = charge/time (ampere); potential difference in volt; resistance in ohm.
  - Ohm's law V = IR holds for ohmic conductors at constant temperature. A 12 V source across 4 ohm drives 3 A.
  - Resistance R = ρL/A: doubling the length doubles R; doubling the area halves R. Metals have positive temperature coefficient (R rises with temperature).
  - Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ (2 + 3 + 5 = 10 ohm). Parallel: 1/R = Σ 1/Rᵢ (two 6 ohm in parallel = 3 ohm).
  - Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R; 220 V at 5 A gives 1100 W. Energy E = Pt.
  - Commercial unit: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. A 2 kW heater for 3 h uses 6 units.
- **Domestic circuits and safety**
  - India supplies 230 V, 50 Hz AC; appliances are connected in parallel so each gets full voltage.
  - Fuse: thin low-melting-point wire in series; melts on overload. MCB does the same job and can be reset.
  - Earth wire carries leakage current to ground to prevent shock.
- **Capacitors**

| Arrangement | Equivalent capacitance |
|---|---|
| Parallel | C = C₁ + C₂ (2 + 3 = 5 µF) |
| Series | 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (6 and 3 µF give 2 µF) |

  - C = Q/V; a 10 µF capacitor at 100 V holds 1 mC. Energy U = ½CV².
  - SI unit farad; practical values in µF, nF, pF.
- **Magnetism and electromagnetism**
  - Oersted (1820): current produces a magnetic field; field lines around a straight wire are concentric circles.
  - Force on a current-carrying conductor in a field: F = BIL sinθ; direction by Fleming's left-hand rule (electric motor).
  - Fleming's right-hand rule gives direction of induced current (generator).
  - Units: magnetic field in tesla (T), magnetic flux in weber (Wb).
  - Faraday's law: induced emf equals rate of change of magnetic flux. Lenz's law: induced current opposes the cause; it is conservation of energy.
  - Generator converts mechanical energy to electrical; motor converts electrical to mechanical.
  - Transformer: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. With 100 primary turns, 500 secondary turns and 20 V input, output is 100 V. It cannot work on DC because a steady current gives no changing flux.
- **Semiconductors and electronics**
  - Intrinsic semiconductors (Si, Ge) are tetravalent. Their resistance falls as temperature rises, opposite to metals.
  - n-type: doped with pentavalent atoms (phosphorus, arsenic); majority carriers electrons. p-type: doped with trivalent atoms (boron, aluminium); majority carriers holes.
  - PN junction: depletion region forms with a barrier potential (about 0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge).
  - Forward bias conducts; reverse bias blocks (tiny leakage). So a diode is a rectifier (AC to DC).
  - Zener diode operates in reverse breakdown and acts as a voltage regulator; LED emits light when forward biased; photodiode and solar cell work on light.
  - Transistor (BJT): emitter, base, collector; used as amplifier and as electronic switch; logic gates are built from transistors.
- **Modern physics basics**
  - Photon energy E = hν; photoelectric effect explained by Einstein (Nobel 1921); it supports the particle nature of light.
  - Radioactivity discovered by Becquerel. After each half-life, half of the nuclei remain: 80 g with a 10-day half-life leaves 10 g after 30 days.
  - Fission splits heavy nuclei (nuclear reactors); fusion joins light nuclei (Sun).
- **Likely question angles:** series/parallel resistance and capacitor numericals; electricity bill in units; which rule or law applies to motor, generator and transformer; n-type versus p-type doping; diode as rectifier, Zener as regulator; half-life and photoelectric effect basics.

topics.title: Management Information Systems (MIS)
topics.theory:
- **Information system types**: **TPS** (routine transactions), **MIS** (summary and exception reports), **DSS** (semi-structured decisions, what-if models), **EIS/ESS** (strategic, executive dashboards), **ES** (knowledge base plus inference engine).
- **Management levels**: operational (detailed, structured, daily data), middle/tactical (summaries, trends, control), top/strategic (external, unstructured, long-term information).
- **Decision types** (Simon): structured/programmed, semi-structured, unstructured; Simon's stages are **intelligence, design, choice** (later implementation).
- **SDLC phases**: planning/feasibility, analysis, design, implementation (coding, testing, conversion), maintenance; models include **waterfall**, **prototyping**, spiral and agile.
- **Feasibility** study covers technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule aspects; **DFDs** and data dictionaries document the analysis.
- **Conversion strategies**: direct cutover, **parallel**, phased and pilot; parallel running is the safest but costly.
- **MIS in functional areas**: finance (budgeting), marketing (sales analysis, forecasting), HR (payroll, attendance), production (inventory, scheduling).
- **Enterprise systems**: **ERP** integrates all functions on one database; **CRM** manages customer relationships; **SCM** manages flow from suppliers to customers.
- **Data support**: DBMS reduces redundancy, **primary key** identifies a record, **data warehouse** is subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile; **OLAP** and **data mining** enable analysis.
- **Security**: **CIA triad** (confidentiality, integrity, availability); threats include phishing, malware, hacking; controls include firewalls, encryption, authentication and backups.

qs.stem: Which information system is primarily used to record day-to-day business events such as sales billing and payroll?
qs.sol: A TPS captures and processes routine transactions at the operational level, and its data feeds higher-level systems. Next, an examiner may ask the difference between batch and real-time processing.

qs.stem: A system that uses analytical models and what-if analysis to help managers solve semi-structured problems is a
qs.sol: DSS combines data, models and an interactive interface for semi-structured decisions. Do not confuse it with an EIS, which gives executives summary and drill-down views.

qs.stem: Which system is designed for senior executives to monitor overall performance through dashboards and drill-down facilities?
qs.sol: EIS/ESS supports strategic, largely unstructured decisions using internal summaries and external data. Key features are graphical dashboards and drill-down.

qs.stem: The two main components of an expert system are
qs.sol: The knowledge base holds rules and facts; the inference engine applies them to reach conclusions. Related terms: user interface and explanation facility.

qs.stem: Which type of information is most needed by top (strategic) management?
qs.sol: Strategic planners need aggregated and external information on markets, competitors and trends. Operational managers need detailed, internal, frequent data.

qs.stem: In the system development life cycle, the phase that immediately follows system analysis is
qs.sol: Typical order: planning and feasibility, analysis, design, implementation, maintenance. Analysis finds what is needed, and design specifies how it will be built.

qs.stem: A feasibility study of a proposed information system does NOT usually examine

opts.A: the personal preferences of the programmers

qs.sol: Feasibility covers technical, economic, operational (plus legal and schedule) aspects. Individual programmer preferences are not a feasibility dimension.

qs.stem: In the prototyping approach to system development,

opts.A: a working model is built early and refined using user feedback
opts.B: each phase is finished completely before the next begins
opts.C: the system is purchased as readymade software only
opts.D: no user involvement is permitted until final delivery

qs.sol: Prototyping reduces requirement misunderstanding through iteration. The sequential approach described in the second option is the waterfall model.

qs.stem: The model in which each SDLC phase is completed before the next one begins, with little backtracking, is called the
qs.sol: Waterfall is linear and sequential, suiting well-understood requirements. Spiral adds risk analysis, and agile uses short iterative cycles.

qs.stem: An ERP system is best described as

opts.A: integrated software that manages the functions of the whole enterprise on a common database
opts.B: a hardware device for network routing
opts.C: a tool only for designing web pages
opts.D: a system limited to the finance department

qs.sol: ERP modules (finance, HR, production, sales) share one database, removing data silos. SAP and Oracle are examples.

qs.stem: A CRM system mainly helps an organisation to

opts.C: manage movement of raw materials from suppliers
opts.D: manage and analyse interactions with customers to improve retention and sales

qs.sol: CRM stores customer data, history and contacts to personalise service. Managing suppliers and logistics is the job of SCM.

qs.stem: Supply Chain Management (SCM) focuses on

opts.D: coordinating the flow of goods, information and finance from suppliers to customers

qs.sol: SCM spans procurement, production, warehousing and distribution. Linking SCM with ERP gives visibility of inventory and orders.

qs.stem: A data warehouse is typically described as

opts.D: limited to a single operational application

qs.sol: These four properties are the classic definition by Inmon. Data are loaded and read but not routinely changed, which supports historical analysis.

qs.stem: OLAP tools are mainly used for

opts.A: recording each sale at the point of sale
opts.D: multidimensional analysis of data such as slicing, dicing and drill-down

qs.sol: OLAP lets analysts view data by many dimensions (time, product, region). It sits on a data warehouse, unlike OLTP, which handles transactions.

qs.stem: The CIA triad of information security stands for
qs.sol: Confidentiality prevents disclosure, integrity prevents unauthorised change and availability ensures timely access. Encryption supports confidentiality and backups support availability.

qs.stem: Phishing is best classified as

opts.A: a social engineering attack that tricks users into revealing sensitive data

qs.sol: Phishing uses fake emails or sites to steal credentials. Awareness training and email filtering are the main controls.

qs.stem: A firewall is used in an information system to

opts.A: increase the storage of a database
opts.B: filter network traffic according to security rules

qs.sol: A firewall monitors incoming and outgoing packets and allows or blocks them. It does not replace antivirus or encryption.

qs.stem: Which of the following is an application of MIS in the human resource function?
qs.sol: Payroll and attendance belong to HR. Sales forecasting is marketing, inventory control is production or materials, and budgeting is finance.

qs.stem: A decision that is routine, repetitive and handled by a well-defined procedure is called a
qs.sol: Herbert Simon classified such routine decisions as programmed; they can be automated, e.g. reordering stock at a fixed level. Unstructured decisions need judgement.

qs.stem: In a typical organisation, the output of a TPS is

opts.A: used as input by MIS and other higher-level systems

qs.sol: TPS data feed MIS for summary and exception reports, then DSS and EIS. This layered flow is often drawn as the pyramid model.

qs.stem: An exception report

opts.C: lists every transaction of the period
opts.D: is produced only once at system design

qs.sol: Exception reporting supports management by exception: attention goes to unusual items only, such as stock below the reorder level.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of an information system?
qs.sol: An information system comprises hardware, software, data, people and procedures. Weather is not a component.

qs.stem: In system conversion, running the old and new systems simultaneously for a period is called
qs.sol: Parallel running is the safest method since the old system is a fallback, but it is the costliest. Direct cutover replaces the old system at once and carries the greatest risk.

qs.stem: Which processing mode is most suitable for an airline seat reservation system?
qs.sol: Seat availability must be updated instantly to avoid double booking, so online real-time processing is required. Payroll is a classic batch example.

qs.stem: A key advantage of using a DBMS in an MIS is

opts.A: elimination of the need for backups
opts.B: reduced data redundancy and improved data consistency

qs.sol: A DBMS centralises data and enforces integrity rules so applications share a single copy. Backups are still necessary.

qs.stem: In a relational database, an attribute (or set of attributes) that uniquely identifies each record in a table is the
qs.sol: A primary key is unique and non-null. A foreign key refers to the primary key of another table to link records.

qs.stem: According to Herbert Simon, the correct order of the decision-making stages is
qs.sol: Intelligence identifies the problem, design develops alternatives and choice selects one; implementation was added later. The order is a frequent exam item.

qs.stem: A Data Flow Diagram (DFD) is mainly used in the system

opts.B: testing phase to detect syntax errors
opts.D: analysis phase to show how data move between processes, stores and external entities

qs.sol: DFDs graphically model processes, data stores, data flows and external entities. Related tools are the data dictionary and ER diagram.

qs.stem: Data mining refers to

opts.B: discovering hidden patterns and relationships in large volumes of data
opts.C: deleting old files to save space

qs.sol: Data mining uses statistics and machine learning on warehouses to find patterns such as customer segments or fraud. It supports DSS and CRM analytics.

qs.stem: The primary objective of a Management Information System is to

opts.A: supply timely and relevant information to support managerial decision making

qs.sol: An MIS gives the right information to the right person at the right time. Information quality criteria include accuracy, timeliness and relevance.

topics.deep:
- **Information and MIS basics**
  - Data are raw facts; information is processed data with meaning. Good information is accurate, timely, relevant, complete and economical.
  - An **MIS** gives the right information to the right person at the right time to support decision making. It draws on TPS data and produces summary, scheduled, ad hoc and exception reports.
  - System components: hardware, software, data, people, procedures.
  - Characteristics of an MIS: management oriented, integrated, uses a common database, supports planning, control and operations, and flexible enough to change with the organisation.
  - Information flows upward as summary and downward as instructions and targets; lateral flow links departments.
- **Types of information systems**

| System | Users | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| TPS | Operational staff | Record daily transactions (billing, payroll, reservations) |
| MIS | Middle managers | Summary and exception reports for control |
| DSS | Middle/senior managers | Semi-structured problems, models, what-if, simulation |
| EIS / ESS | Senior executives | Strategic dashboards, drill-down, external data |
| ES | Specialists, non-experts | Rule-based advice using knowledge base and inference engine |

  - Real-time (online) processing updates immediately (airline reservation); batch processing collects and processes later (payroll).
- **Information needs by management level**
  - Operational: detailed, structured, internal, frequent data.
  - Tactical: summarised, comparative, periodic reports and trends.
  - Strategic: aggregated, external, unstructured and future-oriented information.
  - Herbert Simon: decisions are programmed (structured, routine) or non-programmed (unstructured). Decision-making stages: intelligence, design, choice.
- **System development**
  - SDLC: planning and feasibility, analysis, design, implementation (coding, testing, conversion), maintenance.
  - Feasibility types: technical, economic, operational, legal, schedule.
  - Waterfall is sequential; prototyping builds a working model early and refines it from user feedback; spiral adds risk analysis; agile uses short iterations.
  - Analysis tools: data flow diagrams, flowcharts, ER diagrams, decision tables, data dictionary.
  - Conversion: direct cutover (riskiest), parallel (old and new together, safest), phased, pilot.
- **MIS in functional areas**
  - Finance: budgeting, ledgers, cash flow. Marketing: sales analysis, forecasting, market research. HR: payroll, attendance, recruitment. Production: inventory, scheduling, quality control.
- **Enterprise systems**
  - **ERP** integrates modules on a single database (examples SAP, Oracle). **CRM** tracks customer interactions to improve retention. **SCM** coordinates suppliers, production and distribution.
- **Data management for MIS**
  - DBMS reduces redundancy and improves consistency; a primary key uniquely identifies a record.
  - A data warehouse stores integrated historical data (subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, non-volatile) for analysis; OLAP gives multidimensional analysis; data mining finds hidden patterns.
- **Security and control**
  - CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability.
  - Threats: viruses, phishing (a social engineering attack), hacking, denial of service. Controls: firewall, encryption, passwords and biometrics, access control, backups, audit trails.
- **Likely question angles:** match TPS/MIS/DSS/EIS/ES to users; which system supports unstructured strategic decisions; order of SDLC phases; parallel versus direct conversion; ERP versus CRM versus SCM; data warehouse characteristics; CIA triad; DFD and prototyping definitions.

topics.title: Knowledge Management & New Economy
topics.theory:
- **DIKW hierarchy**: data (raw facts) to information (data with context) to knowledge (information plus experience and judgement) to wisdom.
- **Tacit knowledge** (Polanyi) is personal, experience-based and hard to articulate, like riding a bicycle; **explicit knowledge** is codified in manuals, documents and databases.
- **SECI model** (Nonaka and Takeuchi): **Socialization** (tacit to tacit), **Externalization** (tacit to explicit), **Combination** (explicit to explicit), **Internalization** (explicit to tacit).
- **KM cycle**: create/capture, organise/store, share/disseminate, apply/use, with feedback and renewal.
- **KM tools**: repositories and databases, intranets and wikis, groupware, communities of practice, expert locators (yellow pages), data mining and search.
- **Organisational memory** and **best practices** prevent reinventing the wheel; the **learning organisation** (Peter Senge) continually creates and shares knowledge.
- **Knowledge economy**: knowledge and skills, not land or physical capital, drive growth; ICT, innovation and human capital are central.
- **Digital economy** (term popularised by Don Tapscott, 1995) is economic activity based on digital networks; **network effects** (Metcalfe's law: value grows with the square of users).
- **E-business** covers all online business processes, wider than **e-commerce** (buying and selling); models: B2B, B2C, C2C, G2C.
- **Intellectual capital** = human capital + structural capital + relational capital; **intellectual property** includes patents, copyrights, trademarks and trade secrets.

qs.stem: In the DIKW hierarchy, information is best described as

opts.A: data that has been processed and given context and meaning
opts.C: experience combined with judgement used to take action
opts.D: sound judgement derived from long experience

qs.sol: Data are raw facts, information is data in context, knowledge adds experience and understanding, and wisdom is judgement. Typical question: arrange the four in ascending order.

qs.stem: Tacit knowledge is knowledge that is

opts.A: personal, based on experience and difficult to articulate or codify

qs.sol: The concept is from Michael Polanyi: we know more than we can tell. Skills such as riding a bicycle are classic examples.

qs.stem: Which of the following is an example of explicit knowledge?

opts.B: A teacher's classroom judgement built over years
opts.C: A craftsman's intuition about the right moment to remove metal from a furnace
opts.D: A written standard operating procedure manual

qs.sol: Explicit knowledge is codified and can be documented and shared easily. The other three are tacit and learned through experience.

qs.stem: The SECI model of knowledge creation was proposed by
qs.sol: Ikujiro Nonaka and Hirotaka Takeuchi presented it in The Knowledge-Creating Company (1995). SECI stands for Socialization, Externalization, Combination and Internalization.

qs.stem: In the SECI model, Socialization is the conversion of
qs.sol: Socialization shares experience directly through observation, mentoring and apprenticeship, without writing anything down.

qs.stem: Externalization in the SECI model refers to converting
qs.sol: Externalization articulates tacit ideas as metaphors, models or documents, for example writing a best-practice guide from an expert's experience.

qs.stem: Combination in the SECI model involves

opts.B: merging and organising different pieces of explicit knowledge into a new set

qs.sol: Combination is explicit to explicit, such as compiling reports into a database or consolidating spreadsheets. It is supported strongly by IT tools.

qs.stem: Internalization in the SECI model is best illustrated by

opts.A: a manager writing down a procedure from memory
opts.B: two colleagues sharing experience over lunch
opts.C: an employee studying a manual and practising until the skill becomes second nature

qs.sol: Internalization is explicit to tacit: learning by doing turns documented knowledge into personal know-how. It is the final quadrant of the spiral.

qs.stem: The book 'The Knowledge-Creating Company' is authored by
qs.sol: Published in 1995, it introduced the SECI model. Peter Senge wrote The Fifth Discipline, and Tapscott wrote The Digital Economy.

qs.stem: The phrase 'we know more than we can tell' is associated with
qs.sol: Polanyi introduced the idea of tacit knowing. It underlies the distinction between tacit and explicit knowledge in KM.

qs.stem: Which sequence correctly represents the basic knowledge management cycle?
qs.sol: KM generally involves creating or capturing knowledge, organising it in repositories, sharing it and applying it, with feedback leading to new knowledge.

qs.stem: A lessons-learned database or best-practice repository is mainly a KM tool for

opts.B: capturing and reusing explicit organisational knowledge

qs.sol: Such repositories preserve experience from projects so that later teams avoid repeated mistakes, forming organisational memory.

qs.stem: A 'community of practice' is

opts.A: a group of people who share a profession or interest and learn together by interacting regularly

qs.sol: Communities of practice help to spread tacit knowledge through discussion and shared problem solving. Etienne Wenger is associated with the concept.

qs.stem: An 'expert locator' or 'yellow pages' system in KM helps employees to

opts.B: identify who in the organisation has specific expertise

qs.sol: It maps skills and experience to people so tacit knowledge can be reached through direct contact.

qs.stem: A knowledge economy is one in which

opts.A: growth depends only on land and raw materials
opts.B: knowledge and intellectual assets are the main drivers of growth and wealth
opts.C: agriculture is the only source of income

qs.sol: In a knowledge economy, education, R&D, innovation and ICT matter more than physical resources.

qs.stem: The term 'digital economy' was popularised in the 1990s by
qs.sol: Don Tapscott's 1995 book The Digital Economy described networked intelligence reshaping business.

qs.stem: Which statement correctly differentiates e-business from e-commerce?

opts.A: E-business covers all online business processes, while e-commerce is mainly buying and selling online
opts.B: They are identical in every respect
opts.C: E-commerce is wider and includes e-business
opts.D: E-business refers only to government services

qs.sol: E-business includes supply chain management, CRM, e-procurement and internal operations in addition to online sales.

qs.stem: An online marketplace such as OLX, where individuals sell used goods to other individuals, is an example of the
qs.sol: Consumer-to-consumer platforms connect individual sellers with individual buyers. B2C would be a retailer selling directly to customers.

qs.stem: Intellectual capital is generally classified into

opts.A: human capital, structural capital and relational capital
opts.B: fixed capital, working capital and venture capital
opts.C: debt capital, equity capital and share capital
opts.D: physical, financial and natural capital only

qs.sol: Human capital is employee skills, structural capital is processes, databases and IP, and relational capital is customer and partner relationships.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT an intellectual property right?
qs.sol: Patents protect inventions, copyrights protect creative works and trademarks protect brand identity. A fixed deposit is a financial instrument.

qs.stem: Software that lets geographically separated team members collaborate, share documents and schedule work together is called
qs.sol: Groupware (collaboration software) supports communication, coordination and joint authoring, hence it is a KM tool. Examples include shared workspaces and intranet portals.

qs.stem: According to Metcalfe's law, if the number of users of a network rises from 10 to 20, its value rises by a factor of about
qs.sol: Value is proportional to n², so (20/10)² = 4. This is a key reason for network effects in the digital economy.

qs.stem: Moore's law, relevant to the new economy, states that

opts.A: the value of a network is the square of its users
opts.C: the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every two years
opts.D: the cost of storage doubles every year

qs.sol: Gordon Moore's observation explains falling computing costs. Metcalfe's law concerns network value, not hardware.

qs.stem: The 'digital divide' refers to

opts.A: the difference between analog and digital clocks
opts.B: a break in a fibre-optic cable
opts.C: the gap between those who have access to ICT and those who do not
opts.D: a division of a hard disk into partitions

qs.sol: It reflects inequality of access to the internet, devices and digital skills across regions, income groups or genders.

qs.stem: Compared with raw data, information is more useful to a decision maker because it

opts.C: has been processed and organised in a meaningful context

qs.sol: Processing adds structure and meaning, such as turning sales entries into a monthly trend. Information is still dependent on the quality of the underlying data.

qs.stem: One major aim of knowledge management is to

opts.B: keep all knowledge confidential with individuals
opts.D: preserve organisational memory and prevent the loss of expertise when employees leave

qs.sol: Retaining and reusing knowledge reduces duplication and dependence on individuals. A follow-up could ask which KM tool supports this goal.

qs.stem: A 'best practice' in the KM context is

opts.B: a proven method or process that has yielded superior results and is shared for reuse
opts.C: the cheapest possible approach regardless of quality

qs.sol: Capturing and spreading best practices is a central KM activity, for example through lessons-learned databases and communities of practice.

qs.stem: The book 'The Fifth Discipline', which popularised the idea of the learning organisation, was written by
qs.sol: Senge's five disciplines are personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning and systems thinking.

qs.stem: Skills such as swimming or riding a bicycle are examples of
qs.sol: Such skills are acquired through practice and are difficult to put fully into words, which makes them tacit. Instruction manuals capture only part of them.

qs.stem: India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI), an important digital-economy platform, was developed by
qs.sol: NPCI, set up with RBI and the Indian Banks' Association, built UPI for instant interbank mobile payments. SEBI regulates securities markets, IRDAI insurance, and NABARD agricultural credit.

topics.deep:
- **Data, information, knowledge**
  - Data: raw, unorganised facts. Information: data processed with context and meaning. Knowledge: information combined with experience, values and insight that guides action. Wisdom: sound judgement applied to knowledge (the DIKW pyramid).
  - Knowledge management (KM) is the systematic process of creating, capturing, sharing and applying knowledge to improve organisational performance and learning.
- **Tacit and explicit knowledge**

| Feature | Tacit | Explicit |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Personal, experience-based, intuition | Codified, formal, documented |
| Transfer | Difficult; through apprenticeship and conversation | Easy; through documents and databases |
| Example | Skill of riding a bicycle; a master craftsman's know-how | Manuals, policies, databases, reports |

  - Michael Polanyi: "we know more than we can tell".
- **SECI model (Nonaka and Takeuchi, 1995, The Knowledge-Creating Company)**
  - Socialization: tacit to tacit (shared experience, mentoring, apprenticeship).
  - Externalization: tacit to explicit (articulating ideas as concepts, metaphors, models).
  - Combination: explicit to explicit (merging and organising documents, databases).
  - Internalization: explicit to tacit (learning by doing from manuals and training).
  - The cycle forms a spiral of knowledge creation across individual, group and organisation.
- **KM process and tools**
  - Cycle: capture/create, organise/store, share/disseminate, apply/use.
  - Technology: document repositories, intranet portals, wikis, groupware, search engines, data warehousing and data mining, expert locators (yellow pages), e-learning.
  - Social mechanisms: communities of practice, mentoring, after-action reviews, lessons-learned databases, knowledge audits.
  - Benefits: organisational memory, avoiding duplication of effort, faster decisions, innovation, and spread of best practices.
  - Peter Senge's The Fifth Discipline describes the learning organisation with five disciplines including systems thinking and shared vision.
- **Knowledge economy and new economy**
  - Knowledge economy: production and growth rely mainly on intellectual assets, skills, R&D and ICT instead of land and physical capital.
  - Digital economy: economic activity enabled by internet and digital technologies; Don Tapscott popularised the term in 1995.
  - Network effects: Metcalfe's law says the value of a network is proportional to the square of its users, so doubling users gives about four times the value. Moore's law (transistor count doubling roughly every two years) drove falling hardware costs.
  - Digital divide: gap between those with and without access to ICT.
  - India examples: Digital India (launched 2015), UPI developed by NPCI, e-governance portals.
- **E-business**
  - E-commerce is online buying and selling; e-business is wider and includes supply chain, CRM, e-procurement and internal processes.
  - Models: B2B (supplier to manufacturer), B2C (online retailer to consumer), C2C (OLX, classified marketplaces), G2C (government services).
- **Intellectual capital**
  - Human capital (skills, experience), structural capital (processes, databases, culture, IP) and relational capital (customers, suppliers, brand).
  - Intellectual property: patents (inventions), copyrights (creative works), trademarks (brand identity), trade secrets. These are intangible assets that often exceed physical assets in value for knowledge firms.
- **Likely question angles:** DIKW ordering; classifying a given example as tacit or explicit; SECI quadrant conversions; names (Nonaka and Takeuchi, Polanyi, Senge, Tapscott); difference between e-commerce and e-business; components of intellectual capital; Metcalfe versus Moore laws; examples of KM tools.

topics.title: .NET programming
topics.theory:
- The **.NET Framework** is a managed platform with the **CLR** (execution engine) and the **Framework Class Library (FCL)**.
- Source code of any .NET language is compiled by its compiler into **MSIL/CIL** plus metadata, stored in an **assembly** (.exe or .dll).
- The **JIT compiler** converts MSIL to native code at run time; **NGen** pre-compiles it.
- **CTS** defines common data types; **CLS** is the subset of rules that ensures **language interoperability**.
- An **assembly** contains a **manifest** (name, version, culture, references), metadata, MSIL and resources; **shared assemblies** need a **strong name** and go in the **GAC**.
- **Garbage collection** (3 generations) frees managed memory automatically; **namespaces** (System, System.Data, System.Web, System.Windows.Forms) organise types.
- **C#** (.cs) and **VB.NET** (.vb) are fully object-oriented; VB.NET '/' is floating division, '\' integer division.
- **ASP.NET** Web Forms (.aspx) follow a **page life cycle** (PreInit, Init, Load, events, PreRender, Render, Unload); **IsPostBack** distinguishes first load.
- **State management**: client-side (ViewState, cookies, query string, hidden field) and server-side (Session, Application); validation controls include Required, Compare, Range, RegularExpression, Custom, ValidationSummary.
- **ADO.NET**: Connection, Command, DataReader (connected, forward-only), DataAdapter and **DataSet** (disconnected).

qs.stem: In the .NET Framework, what does CLR stand for?
qs.sol: The CLR is the execution engine that loads assemblies, JIT-compiles MSIL, manages memory (garbage collection), security and exceptions. Next: its core services (JIT, GC, type safety, code access security).

qs.stem: Which component converts MSIL into native machine code at run time?
qs.sol: The Just-In-Time compiler inside the CLR compiles MSIL method-by-method on first call into native code. Related: NGen pre-compiles assemblies ahead of time.

qs.stem: The Common Type System (CTS) is mainly responsible for:

opts.A: Defining the data types and rules every .NET language must follow for types

qs.sol: CTS specifies how types are declared and used so cross-language objects interoperate (e.g., VB Integer = C# int = System.Int32). Related: CLS is the smaller subset of rules for language interoperability.

qs.stem: The Common Language Specification (CLS) is:

opts.C: A subset of CTS rules that languages must follow for cross-language interoperability

qs.sol: CLS-compliant code exposes only features all CLS languages can use (e.g., no unsigned types in public signatures). Related: [assembly: CLSCompliant(true)] attribute.

qs.stem: Which statement about MSIL is correct?

opts.A: It is machine code specific to Intel CPUs
opts.B: It is produced only by C#
opts.C: It is a CPU-independent intermediate code produced by .NET compilers

qs.sol: All .NET language compilers emit MSIL (now called CIL) plus metadata inside an assembly. Related: ILDASM disassembles MSIL.

qs.stem: Which tool is used to view the MSIL and manifest of an assembly?
qs.sol: ILDASM (IL Disassembler) shows MSIL, metadata and manifest. Related: GACUTIL installs to GAC, SN creates strong-name keys, CSC is the C# compiler.

qs.stem: The Global Assembly Cache (GAC) stores:

opts.A: Only private assemblies of one application
opts.B: Shared assemblies that can be used by many applications on the machine

qs.sol: Strong-named shared assemblies are installed in the GAC and versioned side by side. Related: private assemblies live in the application folder.

qs.stem: The part of an assembly that describes its name, version, culture and referenced assemblies is the:
qs.sol: The manifest holds assembly metadata and the list of files and references. Related: type metadata describes classes and members.

qs.stem: An assembly must have a strong name to be placed in the:
qs.sol: Strong name = name + version + culture + public key token + signature, created using SN.EXE. Related: strong name prevents tampering and name clashes.

qs.stem: Which is the root base class of all types in .NET?
qs.sol: Every .NET type derives directly or indirectly from System.Object, giving methods like ToString() and Equals(). Related: value types derive via System.ValueType.

qs.stem: The C# keyword int is an alias for which .NET type?
qs.sol: int is always 32-bit signed in C#. Related: long = Int64, short = Int16.

qs.stem: Which is the default file extension of a VB.NET source file?
qs.sol: VB.NET uses .vb, C# uses .cs. Related: .vbp and .frm belong to VB6.

qs.stem: What is the output of the C# code?  int a = 17, b = 5;  Console.WriteLine(a / b + a % b);
qs.sol: Integer division 17/5 = 3, and 17%5 = 2, so 3+2 = 5. Related: in VB.NET '/' gives Double while '\' is integer division.

qs.stem: In VB.NET, what is the value of  7 / 2 ?
qs.sol: VB.NET '/' always performs floating-point division. Use '\' for integer division (7 \ 2 = 3). Related: Mod gives remainder.

qs.stem: What is the output of the C# code?  int s = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) s += i * i;  Console.WriteLine(s);
qs.sol: 1+4+9+16 = 30. Related: ++ and loop-scope of i in a for statement.

qs.stem: Which C# class should be used for repeated modification of a string without creating many objects?
qs.sol: Strings are immutable, so concatenation creates new objects; StringBuilder is mutable. Related: Append() and ToString() methods.

qs.stem: Which C# access modifier makes a member visible only inside the same assembly?
qs.sol: internal limits access to the same assembly. Related: protected internal = same assembly or derived classes.

qs.stem: In C#, which keyword passes an argument by reference and requires it to be initialised before the call?
qs.sol: ref needs an initialised variable; out need not be initialised but must be assigned inside the method. Related: params allows variable argument count.

qs.stem: Which is the correct order of ASP.NET page life-cycle events?
qs.sol: Typical order: PreInit, Init, InitComplete, PreLoad, Load, control events, LoadComplete, PreRender, SaveStateComplete, Render, Unload. Related: IsPostBack is checked in Load.

qs.stem: The Page.IsPostBack property is true when:

opts.A: The page is requested the first time
opts.D: The page is loaded in response to a post-back from a client

qs.sol: IsPostBack lets code run initialisation only on the first request (if(!IsPostBack)). Related: AutoPostBack property of controls.

qs.stem: Default file extension of an ASP.NET Web Form page is:
qs.sol: .aspx is a Web Form; .ascx user control; .asmx web service; .master master page.

qs.stem: ViewState in ASP.NET is stored:

opts.A: In a hidden field named __VIEWSTATE on the page

qs.sol: ViewState is encoded into a hidden field and travels with each request, preserving control state across post-backs. Related: EnableViewState property.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a client-side state management technique in ASP.NET?
qs.sol: Session and Application state are stored on the server; cookies, query string, hidden fields and ViewState are client-side. Related: default session timeout is 20 minutes.

qs.stem: The default timeout of an ASP.NET session is:
qs.sol: Session.Timeout defaults to 20 minutes and is configurable in web.config. Related: modes InProc, StateServer, SQLServer.

qs.stem: Which ASP.NET file is used to handle application-level events such as Application_Start and Session_Start?
qs.sol: Global.asax holds application and session event handlers. Related: web.config stores XML configuration.

qs.stem: Which validation control ensures that two input values are equal (e.g., password and confirm password)?
qs.sol: CompareValidator compares a control with another control or a value. Related: ControlToCompare, Operator, Type properties.

qs.stem: Which validation control checks input against a pattern such as an e-mail format?
qs.sol: RegularExpressionValidator uses ValidationExpression. Related: CustomValidator runs user-written client/server logic.

qs.stem: Which ADO.NET object is a disconnected, in-memory cache of data that can hold multiple tables and relations?
qs.sol: DataSet works disconnected, filled through a DataAdapter. Related: DataReader is connected, forward-only and read-only.

qs.stem: Which ADO.NET command method returns a single value such as COUNT(*)?

- **Architecture layers:** OS -> CLR -> Base Class Library -> ADO.NET/XML, Windows Forms, ASP.NET -> languages (C#, VB.NET, J#, C++/CLI).
- **Compilation flow:** Source -> language compiler -> **MSIL + metadata** (assembly) -> CLR class loader -> **JIT** -> native code -> execution. Each method is JIT-compiled once, on first call.
- **CLR services:** memory management (GC), type safety verification, exception handling, thread management, code access security.

| Concept | Key point |
|---|---|
| CTS | Common data types, value vs reference types, all derive from System.Object |
| CLS | Rules subset for interoperability; CLSCompliant attribute |
| MSIL | CPU-independent; viewed with ILDASM |
| Private assembly | In application folder; no strong name needed |
| Shared assembly | Strong name; installed in GAC with gacutil; side-by-side versioning |
| Manifest | Assembly identity and dependencies |

- **Value vs reference types:** structs, enums and primitives are value types (boxing converts to object on heap); classes, arrays, strings are reference types.
- **C# basics:** `int`=Int32, `long`=Int64, `string` immutable, `StringBuilder` mutable; modifiers public, private, protected, internal; `ref` (must be initialised) vs `out`; `static void Main()` entry point; `using` imports a namespace.
- **VB.NET basics:** `Dim x As Integer`; `/` -> Double result, `\` integer division, `Mod`; `Sub` (no return) vs `Function`; `Handles Button1.Click` binds events; `Option Strict On` forbids implicit narrowing.
- **Windows Forms:** `Form` class; controls Button, TextBox, Label, ListBox, ComboBox, Timer; events Click, TextChanged, Load; `Application.Run`.
- **ASP.NET page life cycle:** PreInit, Init, InitComplete, PreLoad, **Load**, control events, LoadComplete, PreRender, SaveStateComplete, Render, **Unload**. Dynamic controls are created in PreInit/Init.
- **Web controls:** server controls have `runat="server"`; AutoPostBack triggers immediate post-back; Page directive attributes: Language, CodeBehind/CodeFile, Inherits, EnableViewState.
- **State management:**
  - Client side: ViewState (hidden field __VIEWSTATE), Cookies, QueryString, Hidden fields, Control state.

- **Validation controls:** RequiredFieldValidator, CompareValidator, RangeValidator, RegularExpressionValidator, CustomValidator, ValidationSummary; use `Page.IsValid` on the server.

topics.title: Front End Designed Tools
topics.theory:
- **Visual Basic 6.0** is an event-driven **RAD** tool: forms are designed with the **Toolbox**, attributes set in the **Properties window (F4)**, code written in the **Code window (F7)**.
- **Project Explorer** lists forms (.frm), modules (.bas), classes (.cls) in a project (.vbp); **Immediate window** (Ctrl+G) is used for debugging.
- Every control has **properties** (Name, Caption/Text, Visible, Enabled), **methods** (SetFocus, AddItem, Clear) and **events** (Click, Change, KeyPress, GotFocus).
- **Label** uses Caption, **TextBox** uses Text (PasswordChar, MaxLength, MultiLine), **CommandButton** uses Click event and Default/Cancel properties.
- **ListBox/ComboBox**: AddItem, RemoveItem, Clear, ListCount, ListIndex (-1 = none); ComboBox Style 0, 1, 2.
- **Timer** has Interval (ms) and Enabled, fires the Timer event, and is invisible at run time.
- **Data types**: Integer (2 bytes), Long (4), Single (4), Double (8), String, Boolean, Date, Currency, default **Variant**; use **Option Explicit**.
- **Control arrays** share one name and event procedure and are distinguished by the **Index** property; **MDI forms** hold child forms (MDIChild = True); menus are built in the **Menu Editor (Ctrl+E)**.
- **ActiveX controls** (.ocx) are reusable COM components added through Project > Components.
- **VB.NET** IDE uses Solution Explorer, Toolbox and the **Handles** clause; **HTML editors** like Dreamweaver and FrontPage give WYSIWYG design/code views.

topics.title: Numerical Techniques & Interpolation
topics.theory:
- **Errors**: **inherent**, **round-off** (finite digits) and **truncation** (finite approximation of an infinite process); absolute error = |true - approx|, **relative error** = absolute/true.
- **Bisection**: needs f(a)f(b) < 0, halves the interval each step, **linear** convergence, n >= log2((b-a)/e).
- **Regula-falsi** uses the chord: x = (a f(b) - b f(a))/(f(b) - f(a)); **secant** drops the bracketing (order **1.618**).
- **Newton-Raphson**: x(n+1) = x(n) - f/f', **quadratic** convergence (order 2), fails when f' = 0.
- **Fixed-point iteration** x = g(x) converges when |g'(x)| < 1.
- **Gauss elimination** (direct): forward elimination then back substitution; **Jacobi** and **Gauss-Seidel** are iterative and converge for **diagonally dominant** systems; Gauss-Seidel uses latest values.
- **Finite differences**: delta f = f(x+h) - f(x), E = 1 + delta, nabla = 1 - E^-1; nth difference of an nth-degree polynomial is constant.
- **Newton forward** (near start) and **backward** (near end) need equal spacing; **Lagrange** and **divided differences** work for unequal spacing.
- **Integration**: **trapezoidal** (error O(h^2)), **Simpson 1/3** (even n, exact to cubics), **Simpson 3/8** (n multiple of 3).
- **ODEs**: **Euler** (order 1), improved Euler (order 2) and **Runge-Kutta 4** (global error O(h^4)).
